scenes.name: Joy Division
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: De Warsaw, rock pesado con influencias punk, a la desolación ballardiana: la originalidad crece a medida que las canciones se vuelven lentas y ralas, con el bajo de Peter Hook llevando la melodía, la guitarra de Bernard Sumner abriendo huecos, la batería de Stephen Morris rodeando un cráter y Ian Curtis recitando desde «un lugar solitario». Martin Hannett, productor de Factory, convierte el espacio en «control atmosférico» con delays digitales y grabaciones separadas: Unknown Pleasures (1979), con la portada del púlsar de Peter Saville, «Transmission», «Atmosphere». El coqueteo con la imaginería nazi, la epilepsia, los barbitúricos y un matrimonio roto desembocan en Closer, «estar dentro de la cabeza de Curtis», y en su suicidio en mayo de 1980. «Love Will Tear Us Apart» es su primer hit. Los supervivientes empiezan de cero como New Order.

scenes.name: New Order
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Los supervivientes de Joy Division, perdidos tras la muerte de Curtis («Ceremony», Movement), echan a Martin Hannett, aprenden a programar cajas de ritmos con música electrónica italiana y descubren en Nueva York los clubes chic, la emisora Kiss FM, los remixes de Pettibone, el freestyle y el electro. «Everything's Gone Green» (1981) marca el giro; «Blue Monday» (1983) y «Confusion», producido por Arthur Baker, los convierten en una banda de baile. Con Factory abren The Haçienda, inspirada en Danceteria y Funhouse.

podcast.title: "Blue Monday" Conception
podcast.body: As New Order's drummer, Stephen Morris conceived the initial idea for "Blue Monday" in 1982. He acquired an Oberheim DMX, sampled his own bass drum, and programmed a pattern for audiences to dance to after the band's sets. "So drummer Steven Morris came up with an idea. He'd recently acquired an Oberheim DMX drum machine. He sampled himself playing the bass drum on his kit and then loaded that sound into the DMX."

podcast.title: Drum Machine Programming
podcast.body: As the drummer for New Order, Stephen Morris undertook the task of learning how to program the new generation of drum machines. This skill enabled the band to experiment with more complex rhythms, which proved popular with their growing fan base and contributed to their evolving electronic sound. "At the same time, drummer Stephen Morris began to learn how to program the new generation of drum machines, which allowed the band to experiment with more complex rhythms."

podcast.title: Drum Machine in Encores
podcast.body: Stephen Morris's drum machine was utilized by New Order to play automatically during encores, allowing the band members to depart the stage earlier. This practice contributed to the band's innovative development of a more electronic, machine-driven sound. "just turning on Stephen Morris' drum machine and letting it go while everybody walked off stage"

podcast.title: Experimental Drumming on Closer
podcast.body: Stephen Morris contributed passionate and truly experimental drumming to *Closer*, particularly on tracks like "Atrocity Exhibition," moving beyond the rapid and sometimes acid-like rhythms of *Unknown Pleasures* to explore percussion work far beyond conventional drumming. "Stephen Morris en su batería hace trabajos apasionantes y verdaderamente experimentales en este trabajo."

xref.title: "Accident of Laziness" Origin of Dance Sound
xref.body: New Order's groundbreaking electronic sound and worldwide alt-rock influence partly originated from their reluctance to perform encores. They initially played Stephen Morris's drum machine alone as they left the stage, later adding a sequencer for Gillian Gilbert's synthesizers, and finally, Bernard Sumner conceived sequencing Peter Hook's bass line, leading to songs performed largely by machines. "But their worldwide success and the way they changed alt rock forever was due to an accident of laziness."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 9

xref.title: "Blue Monday" Composition & Instrumentation
xref.body: The composition of "Blue Monday" involved a complex setup: a sequencer built by Stephen Morris connected to an Emulator sampler, a Moog Source keyboard for the bass line, and an Oberheim DMX drum machine. Engineer Martin Usher wrote code to synchronize these devices, and keyboardist Gillian Gilbert's accidental inclusion of an extra rest in her handwritten notation was deliberately kept for the added tension it brought to the arrangement. "He built a sequencer that could be connected to the band's new sampler, a keyboard called an emulator. They sampled a choral effect from a craftwork song called Uranium and wrote a bass line using another keyboard called a Mogue source."

xref.title: Collector of Military Vehicles
xref.body: Stephen Morris, the drummer for both Joy Division and New Order, collects surplus military equipment. His collection features several tank-like vehicles, including an FV433 Abbott Self-Propelled Gun equipped with a 105-millimeter gun. This vehicle, which cost the British Army £1 million new, was acquired by Stephen for £4,000. For local errands, he drives a Mark IV Ferret Reconnaissance Vehicle. "He's got something called an FV433 Abbott Self-Pripelled Gun. It has a 105-millimeter gun mounted on it."

xref.title: Evolution of Bass Programming
xref.body: Peter Hook's later work in New Order involved programming bass lines and drum machines with drummer Stephen Morris. This collaborative approach significantly contributed to the band's unique sound, making it greater than the sum of its individual parts. "Later, his work in programming bass lines and drum machines with new order drummer Stephen Morris made that band into something much more than the sum of its parts."

xref.title: Finding a Permanent Drummer
xref.body: The band struggled to find a permanent drummer until August 1977, when Stephen Morris was found. He was the only individual to reply to Warsaw's advertisement for a drummer in a local music magazine, proving to be a good fit. "The next big date in Jordy Vision history was in August, when they finally found a permanent drummer. His name was Stephen Morris."

xref.title: Formation After Joy Division
xref.body: Following the death of Ian Curtis and the honoring of Joy Division's "suicide pact," Peter Hook, Barney Sumner, and Stephen Morris kept their word to dissolve Joy Division and immediately began working on their next project, which eventually became New Order. "So once Ian was gone, Peter Hook, Barney Sumner, and Stephen Morris kept their word. Joy Division was retired, and work was started on the next project, which would eventually be known as New Order."

xref.title: Formation and Name Origin
xref.body: After Ian Curtis's death, surviving Joy Division members Bernard Sumner, Peter Hook, and Stephen Morris discussed their future. Encouraged by their progress as Joy Division, they decided to move forward under a new name. Their manager, Rob Gretton, suggested "New Order" after finding the phrase in a newspaper headline about mass killings in Pol Pot's Cambodia. "Their manager, my name Rob Greten, is the one who came up with it. He found the name in a newspaper headline about the mass killings in Pol Potts, Cambodia. The phrase was new order."

xref.title: Martin Hannett's Production Genius
xref.body: For the "Unknown Pleasures" album, producer Martin Hannett (described as a "genius, but a certified wacko") radically cleaned up the band's sound and created its distinctive drum sound by rebuilding Stephen Morris's kit, reassembling it on the studio roof, and adding echo, reverb, and sound effects, isolating instruments to achieve an intimate yet cold, detached, and distant atmosphere, which became known as "cold intimacy." "Not only did he clean up the band's sound, but he's the guy who found that distinctive drum sound."

xref.title: Origin of "Blue Monday"
xref.body: In 1982, New Order sought a way to end their live shows without performing encores. Drummer Stephen Morris conceived the idea to program an Oberheim DMX drum machine with sampled bass drum sounds, creating a pattern designed to be triggered when the band left the stage, which evolved into the foundation for "Blue Monday." "In 1982, new order was looking for a way to end their shows. They hated doing on-course and would rather spend the time after their set in the dressing room having a few drinks."

xref.title: Search for a Drummer
xref.body: By 1977, Warsaw was ready to make a demo tape but struggled to find a permanent drummer. Stephen Morris was eventually found in August, as the sole respondent to their advertisement for a drummer in a local music magazine. "By 1977, despite the fact that they couldn't find a permanent drummer, Warsaw was ready to make a demo tape."

xref.title: Suicide Pact and Band Dissolution
xref.body: A solemn suicide pact existed among the members of Joy Division, stipulating that if any member were to leave the band for any reason, Joy Division would cease to exist. Consequently, upon Ian Curtis's death, Peter Hook, Barney Sumner, and Stephen Morris honored their word, retiring Joy Division and beginning work on their next project, New Order. "The deal was that should any member leave for any reason joy division would be broken up. So once Ian was gone, Peter Hook, Barney Sumner, and Stephen Morris kept their word."
